5.doc: The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports
5.title: Which report to use
5.content: All three reports come from the same calibrated model and the same calculations. | InverseAudit - The usual report. It needs no site visit, so it suits remote screening, owner reports and planning. | ASHRAE Level 1 - What ASHRAE Standard 211 asks for a Level 1 audit: a site visit, a description of the building, the historical energy use with the benchmark and target, and the measure summary of low-cost and capital measures, with InverseAudit’s executive summary and utility analysis. It leaves out InverseAudit’s measure-by-measure results, which are Level 2’s. Use it when a program asks for a Level 1 audit only: the auditor has far fewer entries to make (about a third as many). | ASHRAE Level 2 - Level 1 plus what the standard asks for a Level 2 audit: the building’s systems (envelope, HVAC, water heating, lighting and loads), an equipment inventory, the end use breakdown, and more about each measure and the package. Use it when a program asks for a Standard 211 Level 2 audit, for example C-PACE financing, LEED O+M or a city’s audit ordinance. | . The standard doesn’t cover remote audits: every level needs a site visit by a qualified energy auditor. InverseAudit’s analysis alone isn’t a Standard 211 audit, which is why an ASHRAE report stays a draft until the auditor’s entries are done. When no program asks for the standard, see If the project doesn’t need to meet Standard 211.

6.doc: The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports
6.title: Choose the report
6.content: . | On Energy Auditing, choose the building. | Next to Download PDF, click ASHRAE Level 1 or ASHRAE Level 2 under Report. | Click Use ASHRAE Level 1 or Use ASHRAE Level 2 to confirm. | . The page reloads with a Site visit tab, and the Download PDF menu lists the ASHRAE report’s parts. Each building keeps its own report type, and new buildings start on InverseAudit. You can switch at any time. The site visit entries are shared by both levels, so moving from Level 1 to Level 2 keeps everything entered and adds Level 2’s entries; moving back keeps Level 2’s entries without printing them. Only the building’s analyzer can switch, and not while the audit is posted: unpost it first. What Level 1 leaves out . At Level 1 the Site visit tab hides Envelope, Water heating, lighting, loads and Equipment inventory. HVAC asks only for the building automation, and Measures and package only for measures without calculated savings. Items to verify are optional, and Facility and contacts doesn’t ask for the building shape or the walls by facing. The Level 1 report’s Analysis is only the baseline model’s energy use by end use, and its Recommendations are only the measure summary: InverseAudit’s before-and-after end-use analysis, monthly costs and use, measure tables, utility rates, savings table and measure write-ups are left out, because a Level 1 audit doesn’t calculate each measure. The Analysis and Recommendations PDFs are the same. The measures are still entered and calculated on the Energy Auditing page, and the measure summary uses their figures. The Level 1 report also leaves out Level 2’s pages: Building envelope, HVAC systems, Water heating, lighting and other loads, Equipment inventory, the walls by facing, the End-use breakdown, Renewable and distributed energy, and Level 2’s Recommendations pages (the review with the owner, the cost breakdown, the Level 2 measure summary, the savings by measure and the QA/QC check, the package, M&V and Level 3). Its cover and compliance form say Level 1.

7.doc: The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports
7.title: If the project doesn’t need to meet Standard 211
7.content: Some clients want the ASHRAE report’s pages without a Standard 211 audit, for example when the audit is remote. On the Site visit tab, open Compliance page and untick This project must meet ASHRAE Standard 211. The box is ticked unless you untick it. With the box unticked: . | Every site visit entry is optional. The entries you make are printed and empty ones aren’t, so the report is never a draft. Each section shows how many entries are made instead of how many are left. | Missing bills don’t make the report a draft. The historical energy use pages still say which bills are missing. | The report doesn’t name Standard 211. The cover says “Level 2 energy audit” (or Level 1), and so does the audit overview. The auditor’s statement certifies that the report is complete and correct, and mentions a site visit only if its date is entered. The tables keep the standard’s layout, but their notes don’t refer to its forms. | The compliance form (Form A) is left out, and so are the entries only it uses: the qualification route, the audits completed and, at Level 2, the Level 1 date. In Download PDF, Cover and compliance becomes Cover page. | . You can tick the box again at any time, and nothing you entered is lost. Like the other entries, it locks while the audit is posted.

8.doc: The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports
8.title: The Site visit tab
8.content: The qualified energy auditor fills in the Site visit tab after visiting the building. Its sections are listed on the left, each with how many of its entries are done: . | Site visit and interviews - The dates, who was there, the areas and systems visited, what was checked, the interviews, operation and maintenance observations, and the main findings for the Executive summary. | Items to verify - What the owner entered and what the calibration found, for the operating hours, setpoints, lighting, heating, cooling, outside air and water heating. Tick Confirmed when the site visit agrees, or write what was found. A ticked item’s figures print as Modeled, verified instead of Modeled, verify. Recalibrating clears the ticks, since the calibrated values can change; what you wrote is kept. | Facility and contacts - Renovations, earlier audits, landmark status, the owner and bill payer, other space types, the occupancy schedule, and the walls on each side of the building. | Envelope, HVAC and Water heating, lighting, loads - What the model can’t know, such as construction, condition, controls and nameplates. | Equipment inventory - The units installed, one row for each unit or group of identical units. | Utility accounts and rates - Account and meter numbers, and the tariffs; and, when a utility isn’t calibrated, the Calibration follow-up (see When a utility isn’t calibrated). | Measures and package - The review with the owner, planned dates, reasons for measures not evaluated, funding, O&M and M&V costs, and the assessment of solar PV and combined heat and power. | Compliance page - Whether the project must meet ASHRAE Standard 211, the building owner, the auditor and their qualification, and the dates the Level 1 and Level 2 audits were completed. | . Each entry saves when you leave it. For tables, click Add a row to add a row and × to remove one. The entries lock while the audit is posted, and only the building’s analyzer can change them. The number on the tab is how many entries are still empty. An entry left empty isn’t printed, and neither is its title. A table or column with nothing else in it is left out too. The exception is the compliance form (Form A): it keeps all its lines, blank where nothing is entered, so it can be filled in by hand. Narratives . Envelope, HVAC and Water heating, lighting, loads each have narratives for describing the building as found, for example “Systems installed” for the HVAC. They’re optional, so a narrative left empty doesn’t keep the report a draft. Measure text and priorities . The reports use InverseAudit’s text for each kind of measure: its comfort, other non-energy and O&M impacts and, at Level 1, the system it changes. Under Measures and package, the auditor can replace that text for this building, and at Level 1 a measure’s priority. The measure summary with Low, Medium and High bands and a priority is Level 1’s form (L1 - EEM Summary). The Level 2 report has the standard’s Level 2 form instead (L2 - EEM Summary), with each measure’s savings, cost, life, ROI and payback. It opens the Recommendations section, as the same table does in the InverseAudit report, where only the non-energy cost savings column is left out. The comfort and other non-energy impacts are in the Level 2 report’s Other impacts and planned dates table.

9.doc: The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports
9.title: What the report adds
9.content: | Where | What | . | Cover | The Standard 211 Level 2 title, the site visit date and the auditor’s statement | . | After the cover | The compliance form (Form A) | . | Executive summary | An audit overview at the top: scope, energy data, method, key dates, contacts, energy use and the recommended package | . | New sections after the Executive summary | Site visit and interviews, Facility description, Building envelope, HVAC systems, Water heating, lighting and other loads and Equipment inventory | . | Analysis | Opens with energy use by end use with all fuels, before and after the measures, and the End-use breakdown of each fuel with each end use’s peak kW, in place of InverseAudit’s electricity end-use charts and tables. Ends with Renewable and distributed energy. The utility rates are in Historical energy use | . | Recommendations | The Level 2 measure summary (the standard’s L2 - EEM Summary) at the top, in place of InverseAudit’s recommendations table, then the measure write-ups, the review with the owner, the cost breakdown (material, labor and markup), the other impacts and planned dates, measures considered but not recommended, the savings by measure and end use with the QA/QC check, the recommended package, where the savings come from, measurement and verification, and measures for a Level 3 analysis | . | Utility analysis | Historical energy use (accounts, rates, the measured data and the benchmark) and Calibration results. A bill whose cost isn’t on the meter data is estimated in grey at the average rate: the year’s cost ÷ use at the building’s rates. InverseAudit’s EUI and costs by year come first only when the building has more than one year of data | . Each figure is marked with where it comes from: Model (the building’s inputs and model), Modeled, verify (estimated by the calibration, for the auditor to check), Modeled, verified (ticked Confirmed under Items to verify), Calculated, or Auditor. Equipment as the model’s totals . The calibrated model simplifies the building’s geometry and systems; for example, it may have one air handler per floor. So the report gives equipment as the model’s totals, such as the total cooling capacity, supply air and fan power. The auditor lists the units actually installed in the equipment inventory, and the report adds up their nameplate capacities next to the model’s totals. When a utility isn’t calibrated . Sometimes the calibrated model can’t match a utility’s meter data, even though it reflects the building as documented. The report then says so, for the owner to check: . | Natural gas or another fuel - when the year’s total of the bills and the model’s, over the same billing periods and with the same weather, differ by more than 5%. | Electricity - when the NMBE is outside the ASHRAE Guideline 14 limit: ±5% for monthly bills, ±10% for hourly data. | . The audit overview’s Method names the utility, and the executive summary says what its bills show against the model, with finding out why as the first next step. Under Calibration results, a section for the utility lists its bills against the model, points out where most of the difference falls and any bill with an unusual period (under 20 or over 40 days), and gives the possible causes and what to check. The utility’s use, end uses and savings in the report are from the model. When the bills are higher than the model, the section also gives what the excess costs a year at the building’s average rate. The Site visit tab then has an optional Calibration follow-up entry under Utility accounts and rates, for what was checked and the owner’s answer. It prints in that section.

10.doc: The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports
10.title: Checks against the site visit and the bills
10.content: The report compares the model with what the site visit found and with the bills, and points out where they disagree, in dark orange. None of these checks changes the model: they tell the auditor what to look at. Three site visit questions. Under HVAC and Water heating, lighting, loads, three optional choices record what a walk-through finds: . | Outside air dampers when unoccupied - Close, Stay open or Not known. Both levels. | Water heater found on site - None, Electric, Gas or other fuel, Heat pump, or Not known. Both levels. | Economizer as found - Its changeover and whether it runs with the compressor. Level 2 only. | . Differs notes. Under Items to verify, a model value that disagrees with the site visit gets a Differs: note, on the tab and in the PDF: . | the dampers, the economizer or the water heater, against the answers above; | an equipment inventory whose cooling or boiler capacity is more than 20% from the model’s; | a gas furnace efficiency or a DX cooling EER below the federal minimum for the year the units were installed. The year comes from the equipment inventory, or else from the HVAC condition or a renovation that names the HVAC. Units under 65 kBtu/h have no federal EER and aren’t checked. | . When the dampers are found to close already, the outdoor-air damper measure says so: Site visit: the dampers already close when unoccupied, so it may save nothing. Confirm or remove it. Rates against the bills. In the utility rates table, each rate gets a line on how the bills compare with it, from at least 6 bills: when it fits, a fixed amount a bill plus a cost per unit, and how many bills come out more than 10% off their cost at the rate entered. For electricity with a flat rate, it also notes demand recorded on the bills with no demand charge, and the tariffs in InverseAudit’s rate database for the state. The measures are valued at the rate entered: to value them at what the bills show, enter the per-unit rate or the tariff in Rates and run the measures again. Gas above the model. When the gas bills are higher than the model (see When a utility isn’t calibrated), the causes start with A gas leak, a safety item to check first. Each bill’s use a day is then compared with heating degree-days (base 65 °F): Heating runs more than documented when the bills follow the weather, A load that runs whatever the weather when they don’t, or both. A gas water heater found on site that the model doesn’t have is listed too. Humid climates. In climate zones 0A to 3A, a setpoint measure with a cooling setback above 80 °F adds a caution to its comfort impact: humidity can build up over long closed periods. Text you changed yourself stays as you wrote it. Report checks. The page header lists what to fix before the report goes out, for example ENERGY STAR score out of date, a completion date before the analysis, or a flat rate entered that’s far from the bills. A stale ENERGY STAR score is recalculated when you open Energy Auditing. Measured first. The executive summary starts with what the bills show, then the model as the building as documented. The ENERGY STAR score and the costs are labelled as the model’s.

11.doc: The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports
11.title: Draft until it’s complete
11.content: While any required site visit entry is empty, or the energy data is incomplete (for example, natural gas is used but there are no gas bills), the report is a draft: . | Empty entries don’t print, so the Site visit tab is where to see which are open. | Every page header says DRAFT, with how many site visit items are open and what data is missing. | The compliance form shows Not yet for the standard’s requirements, and its signature lines are marked not to be signed. | Full report in the Download PDF menu shows how many items are open. | . Enter 12 months of bills for each fuel on the building’s meter data to complete the energy data. See Meter data.

12.doc: The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports
12.title: Download the PDFs
12.content: Under Download PDF, both ASHRAE reports have Full report, Cover and compliance, Executive summary, Site visit and facility, Analysis, Recommendations, Utility analysis and, for US buildings, Appendix A: ESG/carbon. The parts show the same pages as in the full report. The full report leaves out Appendix B (the carbon impact of each measure), which the standard doesn’t ask for; it stays in InverseAudit’s report and on the Recommendations tab. See Reports and PDFs.

13.doc: The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports
13.title: What the auditor still decides
13.content: . | Measures without calculated savings - Keep each, with the reason, or drop it. | Measures not evaluated - Where the building is below the energy code and no measure was run, give the reason. A measure is listed as not recommended, with no reason needed, when the building already meets the code. | Priorities - They come from the payback. The cost, savings and ROI bands are InverseAudit’s, not values from the standard. | Solar PV and combined heat and power - The report sizes them and asks for the auditor’s assessment. Solar PV savings come from the Solar PV measure, when you run it; combined heat and power needs a Level 3 study. | Costs - Material, labor and markup come from the cost table’s shares for each kind of measure. A cost typed in on the Recommendations tab is shown as its total. | . Check the standard’s own reporting forms and the program’s requirements before you submit the report.

15.title: Before the measures are installed
15.content: Until the measures are installed, the Savings Tracking page shows what they would save with the last 12 months’ actual weather, updated each month, and reminder emails say what is being missed. For: AnalyzerWhere: Analysis › Savings Tracking . On this page . | What the page shows | The monthly estimate | Reminder emails | Related | .

16.title: What the page shows
16.content: Once the audit is posted and before tracking starts: . | Tiles - Potential savings and Utility cost over the last 12 months with their actual weather, and the Retrofit cost and Payback of the selected measures. Until the first monthly estimate, the potential savings and the utility cost are the audit’s, for a typical year. | The selected measures aren’t installed yet - What the measures would have saved a month with the last 12 months’ weather and, once the audit has been posted for more than a month, how much hasn’t been captured since then. Start tracking is here; see Start tracking. | Estimated monthly utility cost - A chart of each of the last 12 months, Without the measures and With the selected measures, and when it was last updated. | Selected measures - The audit’s measures with their cost savings a year (from the audit, typical weather), their costs before and after incentives, and all of them Together as the model calculated them together. | Reminder email to the building owner - How often the reminder is sent. | .

17.title: The monthly estimate
17.content: Each month, InverseAudit runs the building’s calibrated model with the last 12 months’ actual weather, without the measures and with the selected measures. The difference is what the measures would have saved. The audit’s own savings use a typical year; the estimate shows the same measures in the weather the building actually had. The estimate updates by itself from the 10th of each month, with the month before. A month’s actual weather is used only from the 10th of the next month: in the first days after a month ends, the weather data for its last days can still be forecasts or averages instead of measurements. To update it now, click Update now next to the chart. It takes a few minutes. | From the 10th of the month, it covers the 12 months up to last month. | Before the 10th, it covers the 12 months up to the month before last, the same as the last update. Last month is added from the 10th. | . Weather that’s already downloaded isn’t downloaded again: each update adds only the days that are new.

18.title: Reminder emails
18.content: The reminders tell people what the selected measures would have saved with the last month’s weather, over the last 12 months, and since the audit was posted. They’re sent after each month’s estimate and stop when tracking starts. | The building owner - The InverseAudit account that owns the building. Choose Monthly, Quarterly or Off under Reminder email to the building owner. Your choice is saved right away. | Your client’s team - When the building has a client, each person on the client’s team gets their own copy, quarterly unless they change it on their own Savings Tracking page or unsubscribe. See What clients see. | . Click Preview the email to see the reminder as it will be sent. It’s available once the first monthly estimate is made. The monthly estimate and the reminders need an active subscription for the building. A month whose estimate fails is tried again the next day, up to three days a month.

20.title: Calculate, update and post
20.content: Try measures on the calibrated model, refresh the report with the results, and post it for your contacts and clients. For: AnalyzerTakes: A few minutes per runWhere: Analysis › Energy Auditing › Measures panel . The building is calibrated, pinned and subscribed. See Run an energy audit.

21.title: Steps
21.content: . | In the Measures panel, choose the measures you want to apply by changing their values. | Click Calculate. InverseAudit runs the simulation with the selected measures and shows the new savings. The report is marked “The report is outdated”. | If the savings meet your expectations, click Update. The report is updated with the new results. This runs an energy simulation for each measure and can take several minutes. | Optionally, click Run AI analysis to rewrite the report’s text with AI. This replaces the text of every report section, including text you edited yourself. | Check the report. If everything is in order, click Post. | .

22.title: When the buttons turn on
22.content: Each time you open the Energy Auditing page, Update, Run AI analysis and Post start grayed out. | Update turns on when a Calculate finishes. | Post and Run AI analysis turn on when an Update finishes. Post also turns on when Run AI analysis finishes. | After Unpost, run Calculate and Update again before you can post. | . To post an audit you updated during an earlier visit, run Calculate and Update again.

23.title: What you’ll see next
23.content: Your client can view the posted report (see What clients see), and the building appears in Portfolio. The Utility analysis tab of the report becomes available. After the audit is posted, Calculate is turned off. To make changes, click Unpost first. Unpost appears only after the audit has been posted.

24.title: If something goes wrong
24.content: "The report is outdated" You calculated new measures but haven’t refreshed the report yet. Click Update in the Measures panel. "Some text in this section was written from older results" The text was written before the last Update, or before the results changed in some other way, for example a new calibration or new utility rates. Its numbers may not match the tables. Click Run AI analysis to rewrite it, or edit the text. Post asks about it too. Text saved before November 2026 is checked against the last Update only. Calculate shows an error Click Calculate again. If the error comes back, contact support with the building’s name. Update or Post is grayed out They turn on only after Calculate (for Update) and Update (for Post) finish during the current visit. See When the buttons turn on. Calculate shows "Complete Your Energy Audit" The building isn’t subscribed. The Energy Auditing page also shows a Not subscribed banner. Subscribe the building, then calculate again. Calculate is grayed out The audit is posted, or you aren’t the building’s analyzer. If it’s posted, click Unpost first.

26.title: Read the calibration results
26.content: How to tell whether the calibrated model is accurate enough, using its goodness of fit. Where: Home › Building setup › Stats and the top of the Benchmarking page .

27.title: Goodness of fit
27.content: If a model is calibrated within the threshold limits, it is considered sufficiently accurate in simulating the physical reality it is intended to represent. These thresholds are a preliminary guide for the building calibration and should not be treated as absolute values. The statistical indices here relate only to the predicted building energy consumption. | CV(RMSE) - How much the model’s hourly or monthly values scatter around the measured values. | NMBE - Whether the model uses more or less energy than measured, on average. | .

30.title: The Stats tab
30.content: Open a calibrated building on Home and choose Stats in the Building setup panel. Fit to the meter data says whether the calibrated model meets ASHRAE Guideline 14, then shows CV(RMSE) and NMBE as gauges: the dark mark is the limit for the building’s meter data, and a bar past it turns orange. A positive NMBE means the model uses less than measured; the caption says which way it goes. Electricity (kWh): . | Measured and Calibrated model, year weather - The meter year’s electricity and the model’s over the same hours (interval data) or billing periods (bills). Their difference is the NMBE. | Calibrated model, typical weather - The calibrated model run on a typical year. This is the baseline the energy audit uses, so it differs from the meter year by the weather too. | . Weather: the climate zone; Calibration weather, the actual weather of the meter year, measured hourly at the building’s location, which the calibration used; and Typical weather, the station of the typical year and its data set (for example TMY3), which the audit’s results are based on. Three charts open from the buttons at the top: . | Heatmap - Each day’s hours as colors, the measured beside the model with interval data. It shows working hours, weekends and gaps at a glance. | Time series - The hourly measured and model lines, to zoom into a week. | Monthly (Monthly comparison) - The meter data and the model month by month: electricity, peak demand and, with gas bills, natural gas. With interval data each calendar month is compared over the hours that have a reading; with bills, each bill against the model over the same billing period, the months the CV(RMSE) and NMBE are calculated from. Each month’s difference is shown above its bars, in red at 15% or more, so a season the model misses stands out even when the year’s statistics look fine. | .

31.title: On the Benchmark page
31.content: The Benchmarking page shows the same two values as bars. The dark mark is the ASHRAE Guideline 14 limit, and the bar turns orange when the value goes past it. The label next to the bars shows whether the calibrated model meets the guideline.

33.title: Check inputs and run calibration
33.content: The calibration tunes your building’s energy model until it matches your meter data. Every benchmark and audit result comes from the calibrated model. For: AnalyzerTakes: 3 to 40 minutesWhere: Home › Building setup . | All four cards on the building are complete: Meter data, Geometry, Systems and Rates. None shows a Pending badge. | You are the building’s analyzer. Other people see the panel in view-only mode. | .

34.title: Steps
34.content: . | On Home, click the building’s card. In the Building setup panel, click Check inputs. The check takes a few seconds and covers your inputs, historical weather data, incentive rates and retrofit costs. Anything that needs fixing is listed on the Issues tab. | When the check passes, the button changes to Run calibration. Choose a Calibration length: . | Quick - About 3 minutes. | Standard - About 20 minutes. Recommended. | Thorough - About 40 minutes. Tests more combinations of model inputs. | . | To get an email when it’s done, check Send me an email when ready. Then click Run calibration and confirm with Run Calibration. | .

35.title: What you’ll see next
35.content: You can leave the page while the calibration runs. The button shows its progress, for example Calibration in progress (45%). When it finishes, it shows Calibration complete, and the Stats tab shows how closely the model matches your meter data: . | Meter data | CV(RMSE) | NMBE | . | Hourly | 30% or less | within ±10% | . | Monthly | 15% or less | within ±5% | . These are the ASHRAE Guideline 14 limits. See Read the calibration results. Next, open Benchmark to see the results. Clicking Calibration complete lets you rerun the calibration. You’ll check the inputs and run the calibration again. When it finishes, its results replace the current benchmark and energy audit results. Entries on the ASHRAE report’s Site visit tab are kept, but the Confirmed ticks under Items to verify are cleared, since they confirmed the old model’s values.

36.title: What the calibration matches
36.content: The calibration runs the model hundreds of times, changing its inputs (schedules, setpoints, internal loads, envelope and HVAC settings) to find the combination that best matches your meter data. Every input is searched, including the schedules and setpoints you entered; the search starts from your values. For single-zone systems it also tries the supply fan’s speed control (constant, two-speed or variable), and for systems with an air-side economizer, its high limit from 60 °F to 75 °F. | Hourly data - Every hour of electricity, scored by its CV(RMSE). Bias is part of CV(RMSE), so as the hours match, NMBE comes down with it; it’s checked against Guideline 14 afterward. The model also has to match the weather-driven part of your electricity, which InverseAudit separates from the schedule-driven part in your data, so the two are split the way your building splits them. Chilled water and steam meter data count when you upload them. | Monthly data - Each bill’s kWh, scored by its CV(RMSE), and peak demand when it’s off by more than 15%. A bill’s peak is the highest 15 or 30 minutes and the model’s the highest hour, so a small difference is expected. Peak demand counts only when every bill’s demand fits its usage: no lower than the period’s average load and no more than ten times it. Otherwise the calibration matches the kWh only. | Gas and fuel bills - The year’s total, which counts as matched within 5%. Each month instead when the bills are actual meter readings, which counts as matched with a CV(RMSE) within 15%. Fuel oil is always fitted on the year’s total. Gas counts for at most a quarter of the score: gas bills are further from what a model can match than electricity. | . The model runs with your meter year’s actual weather: hourly temperatures, humidity, wind, cloud cover and station pressure. The solar radiation, and any hours without measured weather, come from a typical year: TMYx 2011-2025 from the nearest weather station (CWEC in Canada). Buildings that already have a TMY3 typical year keep it. The benchmark and savings use the typical year. Times are in the building’s local standard time throughout. See Supported data formats.

37.content: The Check inputs button is grayed out One of the four cards is still incomplete, or you aren’t the building’s analyzer. The line under the button says which inputs are missing. I need to stop the calibration Click the progress button and confirm with Stop Calibration. The progress is lost, but your inputs are kept, so you can run it again. If it just started, wait about 10 seconds before stopping it. CV(RMSE) or NMBE is outside the limits Check the meter data for gaps or outliers and confirm the systems and schedules. See Read the calibration results. Check inputs warns that a utility rate is far from what the bills cost A rate you entered is more than 25% off the average cost per unit on your bills. Savings are priced at that rate. If the bills’ costs are complete, open the Rates card and click Use the bills’ rate. See Rates from your bills. The warning doesn’t stop the calibration. Correct the bills, or untick the option so the calibration fits the year’s total. See Natural gas and fuel oil. "Calibration failed" Your inputs are saved. Run the calibration again. 67.title: Electricity
67.content: kW and kWh in interval meter data . Interval meter data typically presents energy consumption information in two key metrics: kilowatts (kW) and kilowatt-hours (kWh). Proper interpretation of these metrics is crucial for accurate energy analysis and billing. Definitions . | kW (kilowatt): A measure of power, representing the rate of energy consumption at a given moment. | kWh (kilowatt-hour): A measure of energy, representing the total amount of electricity consumed over a period of time. | . Data conversion . When converting interval data to hourly figures: . | kW values are averaged to represent the mean power demand. | kWh values are summed to represent the total energy consumption. | . Critical Interpretation . Misinterpreting kW as kWh or vice versa can lead to significant errors in energy calculations: . | If 30-minute kW intervals are treated as kWh, annual energy consumption is overestimated by 100% (double the actual kWh). | If 30-minute kWh intervals are treated as kW, annual energy consumption is underestimated by 50% (half the actual kWh). | . These errors, when propagated over extended periods, can result in substantial discrepancies in energy analysis. Data formats for InverseAudit . InverseAudit supports two major data formats: Green Button and CSV. This manual outlines the specifications for each format and how they are handled by the system. Green Button format . The Green Button is a standardized data format designed for easy and secure access to energy usage data. | Format: Standardized, machine-readable | Purpose: Allows utility customers to access their energy usage data in a consumer-friendly format | Handling: InverseAudit reads each reading’s unit and multiplier from the file (Wh or kWh, energy or power), adds 15-minute readings up into hours, and uses electricity readings only. If the building exports solar power, the hourly use is the energy delivered minus the energy sent back to the grid. Times are converted from UTC to the building’s local standard time. | One file per year: a year split across several XML files, or a zipped download, isn’t read. Unzip it, and use one file that covers the year. | . CSV (comma-separated values) format . CSV is a common output format for spreadsheet programs. InverseAudit supports two types of CSV formats and can automatically recognize the type. Horizontal CSV format . | Structure: Horizontal header shows time, First column shows date | Default Unit: kW | Unit Specification: If needed, include “kWh” or “kW” in the first cell of the first column | File Extension: .csv | . Vertical CSV format . InverseAudit supports two variations of the vertical format: . Two-column format . | Column 1: Date and time combined | Column 2: Electricity usage data | . Three-column format . | Column 1: Date | Column 2: Time | Column 3: Electricity usage data | . Data import process . InverseAudit automatically detects the format of the imported file (Green Button or CSV). For CSV files, the system determines whether it’s a horizontal or vertical format. The data is then processed according to the identified format. Best practices . | Keep the data consistent within each file. | For CSV files, keep the structure described above. | With the horizontal CSV format, specify the unit (kW or kWh) if it differs from the default. | . Times and daylight saving . InverseAudit works in the building’s local standard time throughout: the meter data, the weather and the model. Each reading belongs to the hour it ends in. | CSV files can be in standard time or in clock time (with daylight saving). A file with no readings in the hour that’s skipped in spring counts as clock time and is moved to standard time automatically. | Green Button files are in UTC and are converted. | The model applies daylight saving to the building’s schedules where the location observes it, so the HVAC still starts at the clock time people come in. | The charts on Home show standard time, so in summer a reading appears an hour earlier than on a wall clock. | .

110.title: How savings are measured
110.content: The method behind savings tracking: the calibrated model run with each year’s actual weather and the bills’ periods, compared with the bills, the costs used to price the savings, and when a year or its months so far can be measured. For: Everyone with access to the buildingWhere: Analysis › Savings Tracking › How it's measured . On this page . | The method | The baseline model | The weather | The billing periods | Costs | When a year can be calculated | Savings so far | What it doesn’t adjust for | The monthly estimate before tracking | Related | .

111.title: The method
111.content: Savings tracking follows IPMVP Option D, calibrated simulation. For each tracking year, InverseAudit runs the building’s calibrated model twice, both times with that year’s actual weather: . |   | Model | Answers | . | Baseline | The calibrated model of the building before the retrofit | What the building would have used without the measures | . | Expected | The same model with the installed measures | What it should use with them | . Then it compares both with the year’s bills, month by month: . | Savings achieved = baseline - actual bills | Expected savings = baseline - expected | Achieved vs expected = savings achieved ÷ expected savings | . Running the baseline with the year’s own weather is what makes the comparison fair: a hot summer raises the baseline’s cooling too, so it doesn’t hide the savings, and a mild winter doesn’t create savings that the measures didn’t make. Energy saved is the same comparison in energy instead of dollars, for each fuel: (baseline - actual bills) ÷ baseline.

112.title: The baseline model
112.content: The baseline is the calibrated model as it was when tracking started, with its data year and its fit (NMBE and CV(RMSE)) shown under How it’s measured. It’s kept as it is: new baseline bills or a recalibration later don’t change the tracking, so every year is measured against the same building. The expected model adds only the measures ticked under Measures installed. Measures that weren’t installed don’t count, so a measure left out doesn’t make the results look worse than they are.

113.title: The weather
113.content: Each year uses the building’s actual weather for that year, from the same location as its calibration, prepared the same way as the calibration’s weather. The weather is downloaded once: a later run uses what’s already there and adds only new days. A month’s weather is used only from the 10th of the next month. In the first days after a month ends, the weather data for its last days can still be forecasts or averages instead of measurements. This rule applies to the monthly estimates, to Update now, to the savings so far and to calculating a year.

114.title: The billing periods
114.content: When the bills have their last days of billing period, the year is run over the bills’ own periods. Each month’s model use then covers exactly the days of that month’s bill: the year’s weather starts the day after the last bill ended a year earlier, and the model’s months end on the bills’ last days. Without the last days, the year is run over calendar months. Bills that end mid-month then compare with a month that’s partly different, which matters most in the seasons when the weather changes fastest.

115.title: Costs
115.content: The savings are priced in dollars so that the years can be compared and added up: . | Monthly bills - Every kWh and therm, of the baseline, the expected model and the bills, is priced at the model’s average cost per unit when tracking started, shown under Costs. Using one price for all three means the savings measure energy, not rate changes. | Interval data - The baseline and the expected model are priced with the model’s utility rates, demand charges included. The bills’ use is priced at the baseline’s average cost per unit that month. | . The bills’ own costs are used to check the price. When a year’s bills average more than 2% more or less per unit than the model, the page says so, and Rerun the baseline prices the measured years at the bills’ average cost per unit. See When the bills cost more or less than the model.

116.title: When a year can be calculated
116.content: A year can be calculated when: . | All 12 months have their bills, for electricity and, when the building uses it, natural gas. | The weather for its last bill is final: 10 days after the last bill ends, when each utility has all 12 last days of billing period; otherwise from the 10th of the month after the year’s last month. | . For example, a year whose last bills end on February 14 can be calculated from February 24. The Bills dialog says what’s still missing, or from which day.

117.title: Savings so far
117.content: Before a year can be calculated, its months so far can be measured already. They’re the months that have bills, one after the other from the year’s first month, whose weather is final (as above, month by month). They’re measured exactly like a full year, with the weather of the 12 months that end with the last of them, and shown as Preliminary. They aren’t scaled up to a year: a part of a year isn’t a year, because gas savings come mostly in winter and electricity savings more in summer. Preliminary results stay out of the tiles, the total, the PDF and the emails.

118.title: What it doesn’t adjust for
118.content: The measured savings include everything that changed the building’s energy use since the baseline, not only the measures: more occupants, longer hours, new equipment or a vacancy. InverseAudit doesn’t adjust the baseline for these. Note them under Changes this year in the Bills dialog: they’re shown with the year’s results, so whoever reads the results knows what else changed.

119.title: The monthly estimate before tracking
119.content: Before the measures are installed, the same two models run each month with the last 12 months’ actual weather. The difference is what the selected measures would have saved. See Before the measures are installed.

123.title: The three models
123.content: All three models start from your building’s calibrated model, and all three run with the same typical-year weather: TMYx 2011-2025 from the nearest weather station (CWEC in Canada), or TMY3 for buildings that already use it. Using a typical year takes the weather out of the comparison, so a hot summer or a mild winter doesn’t move the scores. |   | Model | What it is | What changes from your building | . | A | Current building performance | Your calibrated model, run with typical-year weather (the weather-normalized model) | Nothing | . | B | Typical operation scenario | Your building operated the typical way for its building type | Schedules, setpoints and how the floors are used | . | C | Code-compliant scenario | Your building built to the selected energy code | The envelope, lighting, HVAC and water heating values the code sets | . B changes only how the building is run, and C changes only what it’s built with, so each score isolates one side of your building’s performance. A: Current building performance . The calibrated model is the model that matches your meter data with the meter year’s actual weather (see Check inputs and run calibration). For the scores, InverseAudit runs it again with the typical year’s weather. This is the weather-normalized model, and it’s the building “as it operates today” in every benchmark result. B: Typical operation scenario . B is your building with its operation replaced by typical operation. The schedules come from the ASHRAE Standard 90.1-2007 User’s Manual (Appendix G, Table G-I, the schedules of Standard 90.1-1989) for your building type. Office, retail, school, hotel, hospital, warehouse and the other building types each have their own. What B replaces: . | Hourly schedules for weekdays, Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays: interior lighting, office equipment (plug loads), miscellaneous equipment, occupancy and domestic hot water use. | HVAC hours - When the fans run, from the same schedules. | Setpoints - 76 °F cooling and 72 °F heating while the HVAC runs, and 90 °F and 55 °F while it’s off. | Infiltration - Follows the typical fan hours. | How the floors are used - Every floor is occupied, lit and conditioned on the typical schedule. Floors you set as running 24/7, as having the lights off or as unconditioned are put back on it. | Dedicated outdoor-air units - Run only while the building is occupied. | . What B keeps from your building: the geometry and envelope, the lighting and plug load densities, the HVAC system with its efficiencies and controls, the outside air, and the water heater. Only the way the building is run changes. C: Code-compliant scenario . C is your building with every value the selected energy code sets replaced by the code’s value, for your climate zone, building type and HVAC system. These are the values of the Energy Code (blue) buttons in the Measures panel; see ECM parameters. What C replaces, where your building has it: . | Envelope - Roof and exterior wall insulation (R-value), window U-value and shading coefficient, and R-30 under a lowest floor over open parking. | Lighting - Lighting power density, and the occupancy sensor controls during occupied and unoccupied hours. | Air-side - DX cooling efficiency (EER), heat pump heating efficiency (COP), furnace efficiency, motorized outdoor-air dampers, minimum outside air, and dedicated outdoor-air units running only while occupied. The air-side economizer follows the code: integrated, with the code’s high limit, where the code requires one, and none where it doesn’t. For VAV systems also: a 30% minimum fan flow and box flow, supply air temperature reset where the code asks for it, and the ASHRAE fan part-load curve. | Chilled water plant - Chiller efficiency (kW/ton), 44 °F chilled water, the pump heads, and turning the chilled water off by outdoor temperature. | Hot water plant - Boiler efficiency, 180 °F hot water, the pump head, and turning the hot water off above 65 °F outdoors. | Water heater - Efficiency: 80% for gas, 96% for electric, and a COP of 3.6 for a heat pump. | . What C keeps from your building: the schedules, setpoints and setbacks (your own operation), the plug and process loads, infiltration, the HVAC system type and capacities, fan operation, supply air temperatures and exhaust. A value the code doesn’t set stays as calibrated. The energy code is the one selected on the Current performance vs. energy code card on Benchmarking; the code currently in force in your state is tagged Current State Code. Only the building’s analyzer can change it. Changing it runs C again and changes the asset score. See Scores.

124.title: The formula
124.content: Energy use intensity . Each model’s energy use intensity (EUI) is its site energy for the year, all fuels together, divided by the floor area: . EUI = (electricity + natural gas + other fuels, in kBtu) ÷ floor area (ft²) . Each fuel is converted to kBtu first: 3.413 kBtu per kWh, 100 kBtu per therm and 137.4 kBtu per gallon of fuel oil. The floor area is the same for all three models, so it cancels out of the scores: they compare total energy use. The scores . Operational score = 100 - 50 × A EUI ÷ B EUI . Asset score = 100 - 50 × A EUI ÷ C EUI . 50 × A ÷ reference is rounded to a whole number first. A building that uses twice the reference or more scores 0, so scores stay between 0 and 100. Only a building that uses no energy would score 100. | Your building uses | Score | . | Half the reference | 75 | . | 20% less than the reference | 60 | . | The same as the reference | 50 | . | 20% more than the reference | 40 | . | 50% more than the reference | 25 | . | Twice the reference or more | 0 | . Example . An office building’s three models use, in kBtu/ft² a year: . | A Current building | B Typical operation | C Code-compliant | . | 80 | 70 | 100 | . | Operational score = 100 - 50 × 80 ÷ 70 = 100 - 57 = 43. The building uses about 14% more than the same building run the typical way: it probably runs longer hours or with tighter setpoints than typical. | Asset score = 100 - 50 × 80 ÷ 100 = 100 - 40 = 60. On its own schedules, it uses 20% less than if it were built to code: its envelope and equipment are better than the code’s. | . Reading the two scores together . The Whole-building performance score card’s standard text reads the pair this way: . |   | Operational score above 50 | Operational score below 50 | . | Asset score above 50 | Performing well in both areas: keep it up with consistent operation and preventive maintenance. | Solid building, operational issues: schedule and maintenance fixes can save quickly at low cost. | . | Asset score below 50 | Operated reasonably well, held back by outdated equipment and systems: capital upgrades have the biggest impact. | Both need attention: start with low-cost operational fixes while planning equipment upgrades. | . When either score is exactly 50, it reads as moderate performance across the board.

125.title: Scores by fuel and by end use
125.content: The End uses tab applies the same formula to parts of the building’s energy, in the End-use performance tables: . | Each end use - Lighting, plug loads, heating, cooling, fans, pumps and the others, each against the same end use in B (operational score) and in C (asset score). Electric end uses are compared in kWh/ft², and natural gas and other fuels in kBtu/ft². | Each fuel - Electricity on its own and the other fuels together, and each energy source in the Energy use scores table. | . A dash (–) means there’s no score: the reference uses none of that end use, so there’s nothing to compare with. The score cells are shaded with the key above the tables: 80 and above, 50-79, 40-49, 30-39 and below 30. An end use with a low operational score points to its schedules or setpoints, for example fans or pumps running at night. One with a low asset score points to its equipment or the envelope. See Scenarios and the energy use gap. The whole-building scores aren’t an average of the end-use scores: they compare the total energy, so the end uses that use the most count the most.

126.title: Scores after the retrofit
126.content: On Energy Auditing, the Score card shows a score now and after the measures. Under Manage, choose which one: ENERGY STAR score, ENERGY STAR site EUI, operational score or asset score. See Run an energy audit. The scores after the retrofit use the same references, B and C, with your building after the measures in place of A. Each score counts only its own kind of measure: . | Asset score after the retrofit - Your building with the envelope and equipment measures only: every measure except the Operations group. Outdoor-air dampers and controls count here, because they take capital. | Operational score after the retrofit - Your building with the Operations measures only: schedules, setpoints, setbacks, floors and the dedicated outdoor-air schedule. | . This way a new setback doesn’t raise the asset score, and new windows don’t raise the operational score. Calculate runs these two models along with all the measures together. If there are no measures of one kind, that score stays as it is now. For a building whose measures were last calculated before November 2026, both scores use all the measures together until you click Calculate again. The card’s note reads the score now: below 40 means significant savings opportunities, 40 to 59 a medium range that still has substantial ones, and 60 or more a building that is well operated (operational score) or well maintained (asset score).

127.title: When the scores change
127.content: . | After a calibration - All three models run again, so both scores can change. | When the energy code changes - C runs again for the new code, so the asset score changes. | When you calculate measures - Only the scores after the retrofit change. | . The scores don’t use your bills directly: they compare models, all with the same typical weather. New bills change them only through a new calibration.

128.title: How they differ from the ENERGY STAR score
128.content: The ENERGY STAR score compares your building with similar buildings nationwide, using ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager. It reflects the building, its operation and its use all together, and 50 is the national median. The operational and asset scores compare your building only with versions of itself. That makes them work for building types ENERGY STAR doesn’t cover, and it tells you which side to work on: the operation or the building itself. As with the ENERGY STAR score, 50 is the middle and higher is better.

154.title: Track savings
154.content: Savings tracking measures what the audit’s measures actually save. 155.title: How it works
155.content: . | Before the measures are installed - The page shows what the selected measures would save with the last 12 months’ actual weather, updated each month, and reminder emails tell the building owner and your client what they’re missing. See Before the measures are installed. | Start tracking - Once the work is done, tick the measures that were installed and enter the month the work was completed. The model is kept as it is from then on. See Start tracking and measure each year. | Enter each year’s bills - Type them or let AI fill them in from the bill files, month by month. See Enter a year’s bills. | Savings so far - While a year is still open, its months with bills can be measured already, as a preliminary result. | Calculate the year - Once all 12 months are in, InverseAudit runs the calibrated model with that year’s actual weather, with and without the installed measures, and compares it with the bills. See How savings are measured. | Share it - Show the results to your client on their Savings Tracking page, and email them when a year is measured. See What clients see. | . The method is IPMVP Option D, calibrated simulation: the savings are the difference between what the building would have used without the measures, in that year’s weather, and what its bills say it used.

165.content: The Meter data card no longer shows Pending. When all four cards are done, check inputs and run the calibration.

166.title: Import utility bills with AI
166.content: The first tab can fill in the fields for you. Upload your utility bills (and, for buildings with hourly data, your interval data file) and click Import and fill monthly data (buildings with monthly data, tab Import bills) or Import and fill meter data (buildings with hourly data, tab Import files). Check the values on the other tabs before you save. The import reads each bill’s usage, peak demand and total cost. The costs set your utility rates: see Rates from your bills. You can upload up to 50 files of up to 40 MB each: PDF, JPG, PNG, XLS, XLSX, CSV, TXT or XML (Green Button), with at most two CSV or TXT files and one Excel file. Importing again overwrites the data on the other tabs.

167.title: Natural gas and fuel oil
167.content: Enter each month’s use on the Natural gas / fuel oil tab: therms for natural gas, gallons for fuel oil. Purchased steam without a meter file is entered here too, in MMBtu. The two options beside the table decide how the calibration uses these bills: . | No natural gas or fuel oil - Sets every month to 0. Tick it only when the building uses neither. If the building heats with gas and you leave its bills out, its heating isn’t calibrated. | Bills are actual meter readings - Tick it when every bill is an actual reading, with no estimated, skipped or combined months. The calibration then compares each month’s bill with the model, against ASHRAE Guideline 14. Left unticked, it fits the year’s total. This option isn’t offered for fuel oil, whose deliveries don’t follow the months: fuel oil is fitted on the year’s total. | . Utilities sometimes skip a month’s reading and bill it with the next one. Enter 0 for the skipped month, not an estimate, and leave Bills are actual meter readings unticked: the next bill makes up the skipped month, so the year’s total is still right and the calibration isn’t misled. With the option ticked, Check Inputs warns about a month billed 0 between two months with gas, unless a cost is entered for it: a month with only a charge, such as a summer customer charge, is a bill. The calibration weighs electricity more than gas: gas counts for at most a quarter of the score, and the gas counts as matched when the year’s total is within 5% (each month’s CV(RMSE) within 15% when the bills are actual meter readings). Gas bills are usually further from anything a model can match than electricity. The audit report’s Appendix A states how the gas was calibrated.

168.title: Time stamps and daylight saving time
168.content: An interval data file is timed either by the clock, which moves an hour for daylight saving time, or in standard time all year. The calibration lines the model’s hours up with the readings, so it needs to know which. The Time stamps box on the Electricity (hourly data) tab shows what InverseAudit found, and you can change it: . | Detect from the readings - InverseAudit compares the building’s weekday start and stop in the weeks before and after each clock change. If they stay at the same hours, the readings follow the clock; if they move an hour, they’re in standard time. Readings without a clear working day are taken as following the clock, as most utilities’ files are. Leave Green Button files on this choice: they’re moved to standard time when imported. | Follow the clock (daylight saving time) or Standard time all year - Choose one when you know how your utility times its files. | . The box appears only where the clocks change. Your choice is kept when you import the interval data again. Changing it sends the building back to preparation, so run the calibration again.

169.title: Missing data and outliers
169.content: Treat readings that don’t represent actual energy use as missing data. Up to 2,500 hours of data points can be missing, and the data must cover at least 9 months. To exclude readings, edit the file in Excel or any text editor and either: . | remove the entire row, including the date, or | fill the readings with zeros or blanks, keeping the dates. | . The examples below are all acceptable in a CSV (comma-separated values) file. For Green Button data, use an XML editor. .

170.title: If something goes wrong
170.content: My interval data file won't import Check that the file matches one of the supported data formats, and that it covers at least 9 months with no more than 2,500 missing hours. If it still won’t import, contact support and attach the file. The annual electricity use looks doubled or halved The file’s unit was probably read as kW instead of kWh, or the other way around. Put the unit in the file as described in Supported data formats. In summer, the model's hours are an hour off the readings On the calibration’s heat map, the calibrated model’s working day starts an hour earlier or later than the measured one while daylight saving time is on. Set Time stamps on the Electricity (hourly data) tab to how your utility times its files, save, and run the calibration again. See Time stamps and daylight saving time.

193.title: Scores
193.content: What the ENERGY STAR, operational and asset scores and the energy cost comparison mean, and how to read them. For: Everyone with access to the buildingWhere: Analysis › Benchmarking . On this page . | ENERGY STAR score | Operational and asset scores | Energy cost vs. energy code | Related | .

194.title: ENERGY STAR score
194.content: The ENERGY STAR score rates your building’s overall energy performance on a 1 to 100 scale, reflecting its physical assets, how it’s operated and how it’s used. A score of 50 is the median: lower is worse than similar buildings nationwide, and higher is better. It helps you decide which buildings to improve first.1 . The card shows your building’s score and site EUI next to the portfolio median (a score of 50) and its site EUI. The site EUI uses the modeled floor area, so it matches the calibrated model. If the model changes, for example after you rerun the calibration, the score is recalculated the next time you open the page. To calculate the score for a different property type, choose it under ENERGY STAR property type and click the refresh button next to it. Some building types aren’t covered by ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager, and no score is shown for them.

195.title: Operational and asset scores
195.content: The operational score and the asset score work like the ENERGY STAR score: 50 means the same energy use as the reference, a lower score is worse, and a higher score is better. Both compare your building with a version of itself rather than with other buildings, so they show which side to work on: how the building is run, or the building itself. | Operational score - Compares your building with the same building run on the typical schedules and setpoints for its building type (ASHRAE Standard 90.1-2007 User’s Manual). For example, if an office building runs longer than the typical weekday schedule, its operational score is lower than 50. Operational score = 100 - 50 × A / B | Asset score - Similar to the miles-per-gallon (MPG) rating used for cars. It compares your building with the same building built to the selected energy code, on its own schedules: insulation, windows, lighting power, and heating, cooling and water heating efficiencies. Asset score = 100 - 50 × A / C | . A, B and C are the three compared scenarios, each as a site EUI in kBtu/ft². Scores range from 0 to 100: using 20% less than the reference scores 60, and 20% more scores 40. All three models run with the same typical-year weather, so the weather doesn’t move the scores. For what each model changes, the rounding, a worked example and the scores after the retrofit, see How scores are calculated.

196.title: Energy cost vs. energy code
196.content: Current performance vs. energy code shows how much higher or lower your building’s energy cost is than the code-compliant scenario, and how the current energy cost is split between energy sources. To compare with a different code, click the energy code’s name and choose another one. The results are recalculated, which can take up to 10 seconds. The code currently in force in your state is tagged Current State Code. Only the building’s analyzer can change the code.

217.content: Click + Add a year to add the next 12 months. The first year starts the month after the work was completed, and each year after it a year later. The Bills dialog opens for the new year; see Enter a year’s bills. | Column | What it shows | . | Year | The 12 months, marked Preliminary while only its months so far are measured | . | Bills | How many of the 12 months have their bills | . | Baseline, this year’s weather | What the building would have cost without the measures, in that year’s weather | . | Actual bills | What the bills’ use cost, at the same cost per unit | . | Savings achieved | Baseline minus actual bills | . | Expected savings | Baseline minus the model with the installed measures: what the measures should have saved in that year’s weather | . | Achieved vs expected | Savings achieved as a share of the expected savings | . 218.doc: Start tracking and measure each year
218.title: Calculate a year
218.content: Once all 12 months have their bills, click Calculate on the year’s row, or Calculate in the Bills dialog. It takes a few minutes. InverseAudit runs the calibrated model with the year’s actual weather, without and with the installed measures, and compares both with the bills. A year can be calculated once the weather for its last bill is final: 10 days after its last bill ends, when the bills have their last days of billing period, or else from the 10th of the month after the year’s last month. Until then, the Bills dialog says from which day. See When a year can be calculated. When the year is measured and it’s shown to your client, InverseAudit offers to email them. See Share the results.

219.doc: Start tracking and measure each year
219.title: Savings so far
219.content: You don’t have to wait for the whole year. While a year is open, its months that have bills, one after the other from its first month and with final weather, can be measured already: . | Click Update so far on the year’s row. It shows when a new month is ready and the year can’t be calculated yet. | From the 10th of each month, InverseAudit also updates the months so far by itself. | . The row is marked Preliminary and its figures are in grey italics. View shows the months so far, with Preliminary: 5 of 12 months, for example, and the months without results empty. Savings so far are measured the same way as a full year, month by month, but a part of a year isn’t a year: gas savings come mostly in winter, and electricity savings more in summer. They aren’t scaled up to a year, and they’re left out of the tiles, the total, the PDF and the emails. The year is final once all 12 months are in and calculated. If you change the bills of a month that’s already measured, the preliminary result is cleared until the next update.

231.title: What InverseAudit does
231.content: InverseAudit is an energy auditing platform for commercial buildings. It builds a calibrated energy model of your building from monthly or interval meter data, without the effort that manual modeling and calibration require.

232.title: The workflow
232.content: graph LR A["Add a building"] --> B["Enter data"] B --> C["Calibrate"] C --> D["Benchmark"] D --> E["Subscribe"] E --> F["Energy audit"] F --> G["Post the report"] G --> H["Track savings"] . | Add your building. | Enter its meter data, geometry, systems and rates. | Run the calibration. InverseAudit tunes the model until it matches your meter data. | Review the benchmark results. | Subscribe the building to unlock the energy audit. | In the energy audit, try energy conservation measures and see their savings and payback. | Post the report so your contacts and clients can see it. | Once the measures are installed, track the savings: each year’s bills are compared with the calibrated model run with that year’s weather. | .

233.title: Why a model should be calibrated
233.content: Energy modeling is not always accurate, especially for older existing buildings. A model’s accuracy is limited by the complexity of buildings. It also depends on operational factors such as schedules and occupancy, how systems and equipment are operated, plug loads and weather.1 A model that hasn’t been calibrated with utility data isn’t accurate, so it should be calibrated before energy cost savings are calculated.

234.title: Why use InverseAudit
234.content: . | It creates and calibrates a model based on your utility data and historical weather data. This leads to an accurate and representative model of your building. | Its analysis has the depth of an ASHRAE Level 2 energy audit: savings and costs for each measure, calculated with a calibrated model. | With the ASHRAE Level 1 or Level 2 report and a site visit by a qualified energy auditor, the report can meet ASHRAE Standard 211 for that level. | . InverseAudit can be used for: . | ASHRAE Standard 211 Level 2 energy audits, with a site visit by a qualified energy auditor | Energy audits for building-ordinance requirements (the audit report; filing happens outside InverseAudit) | LEED O+M: Existing Buildings | .

235.title: Methodologies and standards
235.content: InverseAudit incorporates industry standards such as: . | ASHRAE Standard 90.1 | ASHRAE Standard 211 | IPMVP (International Performance Measurement and Verification Protocol) | . It combines them with its own calibration methods. See How scores are calculated for the models behind the results. To try it, follow the Quick start with the Demo Building. | How Accurate is Energy Modeling in the Market. ↩ . | .

243.content: . | Savings tracking. An open tracking year’s months with bills can be measured before the year is complete, as a preliminary result, with Update so far or by themselves each month. See Savings so far. | Weather from the 10th. See The weather. | For clients, a side menu with Home, Benchmarking (read only, with Download PDF), Energy Auditing and Savings Tracking, where they see the potential savings, the measured savings and the bills you enter, read only, and choose how often they get the reminder email. See What clients see. | Sign in asks “How do you use InverseAudit?” with a card for each role, and the sign-in form shows the choice, with a switch to change it. Google sign-in keeps the choice too. See Sign in and your profile. | Scores after the retrofit count only their own kind of measure: the asset score the envelope and equipment measures, the operational score the Operations measures. How scores are calculated now explains the three models, what each one changes, the formula with an example, and the scores by end use. | ASHRAE report checks. Three site visit questions (outside air dampers when unoccupied, the water heater, and at Level 2 the economizer), Differs notes where the model disagrees with the site visit or is below the federal minimum efficiency, the rates against the bills, the causes when gas is above the model, a humidity caution for high setbacks in humid climates, and report checks in the page header. See Checks against the site visit and the bills. | When a utility isn’t calibrated, the ASHRAE reports say so, for the owner to check, with the bills against the model and the possible causes. Confirmed items under Items to verify print as Modeled, verified. See When a utility isn’t calibrated. | Archive a building you no longer need in your lists, and bring it back with View archived. See Archive a building. | Calibration also tries the supply fan’s speed control for single-zone systems, and the economizer’s high limit from 60 °F to 75 °F. See Check inputs and run calibration. | ASHRAE Level 2 report. On Energy Auditing, choose Report: ASHRAE Level 2 to add the pages ASHRAE Standard 211 asks for a Level 2 audit, including a compliance form, the facility and its systems, an equipment inventory, calibration results and more about each measure. A qualified energy auditor completes them in the new Site visit tab, and the report stays a draft until they’re done. Report: ASHRAE Level 1 gives the Level 1 report, with only the entries Level 1 asks for. See The ASHRAE Level 1 and Level 2 reports. | One table for each set of figures. The Level 2 report no longer repeats the same figures in two tables: the Analysis section opens with the end uses of every fuel and the End-use breakdown (now with each end use’s peak kW), the cost table gives the material, labor and markup, the savings by measure leave the totals to the QA/QC check, and the Utility analysis is the historical energy use, with the EUI and costs by year only for buildings with several years. See What the report adds. | Each level’s own measure summary. The Level 2 report no longer has Level 1’s measure summary with Low, Medium and High bands: it has the standard’s Level 2 form with each measure’s figures, at the top of Recommendations, and each measure’s comfort and other non-energy impacts are next to its O&M impact. See Measure text and priorities. | One measure table in every report PDF. The InverseAudit report’s Recommendations open with the same measure table as the Level 2 report, with each measure’s description, life, ROI and payback, low-cost and capital measures listed apart, and all measures together. The report PDFs no longer print the SIR; the Recommendations tab still shows it. See Reports and PDFs. | A shorter Level 1 report. The ASHRAE Level 1 report’s Analysis is the baseline’s energy use by end use, and its Recommendations are the measure summary, without InverseAudit’s measure-by-measure results, which are Level 2’s. See What Level 1 leaves out. | Bill costs in the ASHRAE reports. On the Historical energy use page, a bill without its cost on the meter data gets an estimate at the average rate (the year’s cost ÷ use at the building’s rates), in grey, instead of a blank and a $0 total. The interval data’s estimate and the Annual summary use the same rate. See What the report adds. | Standard 211 or not. When no program asks for ASHRAE Standard 211, untick This project must meet ASHRAE Standard 211 on the ASHRAE report’s Site visit tab (Compliance page). Every entry becomes optional, the report is never a draft, and it keeps its pages without naming the standard, claiming compliance or printing the compliance form. See If the project doesn’t need to meet Standard 211. | Report PDFs have one layout: every section’s tables have names on the left and numbers on the right, and the ASHRAE reports’ charts match the rest of the report. Natural gas is orange in every chart, the charts sit centred under their titles, and headings are in sentence case. The cover has no page header or footer, and its statement and signatures sit at the foot of the page. Each file’s name starts with the report type, such as ASHRAE Level 2. For the InverseAudit report, Download PDF also has Appendix B: Carbon impact of measures. See Reports and PDFs. | Report fixes. Charts in the report PDFs are always printed in full; on a busy server some used to print half-drawn or blank. Appendix A gives the building’s type, the energy data it covers and the calibration’s results, instead of fixed text. An ASHRAE report’s cover isn’t certified while the report is a draft. Report text written from older results, for example before new utility rates, is flagged on the Energy Audit page and when you post. See Calculate, update and post. | Benchmarking PDF. Download PDF on the Benchmarking page prints the Scores and End uses tabs with every table, chart and analysis. See Understand the benchmark. | The end-use score tables have a score shading key, on the page and in the PDF, and each fuel keeps its own color in the share of energy cost (electricity blue, natural gas orange). See Scenarios and the energy use gap. | The Typical Operation Scenario uses the schedules of the ASHRAE Standard 90.1-2007 User’s Manual for the building type, from the next calibration. See How scores are calculated. | When Benchmarking or Energy Auditing has no building to show, it says why (no building yet, none calibrated, or none pinned) and links to the next step on Home. | Rates from your bills. The AI bill import reads each bill’s total cost, and each rate becomes the bills’ average cost per unit. Check Inputs warns when a rate you entered is more than 25% off the bills. See Rates. | Natural gas. The calibration fits the year’s total gas use, so a month the utility skipped and billed with the next one does no harm: enter 0 for it. If your bills are actual meter readings, tick Bills are actual meter readings to compare each month instead. See Meter data. | Calibration. Hourly calibrations are scored on bias (NMBE) as well as CV(RMSE), as monthly ones are, and gas and fuel bills weigh at most 25% of the score. The search starts from the schedules and setpoints you entered. See Check inputs and run calibration. | Weather. The calibration uses the meter year’s measured cloud cover and station pressure along with temperatures, with the typical year’s solar radiation, and typical-year runs use TMYx 2011-2025 weather from the nearest station (CWEC in Canada). Baselines that already have a TMY3 typical year keep it. | Time. Meter data, weather and charts are in the building’s local standard time. Interval files recorded in clock time (with daylight saving) are converted automatically, and the model applies daylight saving to its schedules. Recalibrate hourly baselines to use this. See Supported data formats. | Green Button import reads the file’s units correctly (a 15-minute Wh file used to come in far too large), subtracts solar export from delivered energy, and uses electricity readings only. | Fuel oil bills are counted in gallons, purchased steam bills now count in the calibration, and chilled water and steam meter data are used in hourly calibrations whenever they’re uploaded. | A billing year that starts on February 29 now covers the full year. | .
